A · Feature Matching Key Terms — Matching

Descriptor distance

/dɪˈskrɪp.tər/ · SIFT: 128 numbers

A descriptor is the list of numbers summarising the patch around a keypoint (Session 5). Nearest = smallest Euclidean distance between two lists: Session 5's SSD, square-rooted.

ระยะระหว่างเวกเตอร์สองตัว · ใกล้ที่สุด = ระยะยุคลิดสั้นที่สุด

Match

/mætʃ/

A pair of keypoints, one from each image, proposed as the same physical point.

คู่จุดจากสองภาพที่เสนอว่าเป็นจุดเดียวกันในโลกจริง

Ratio test

/ˈreɪ.ʃi.oʊ/ · Lowe's ratio

Keep a match only if the best candidate is clearly closer than the second-best.

เก็บคู่ไว้เฉพาะเมื่อตัวที่ใกล้ที่สุดชนะตัวรองอย่างชัดเจน

Outlier

/ˈaʊt.laɪ.ər/

A match that is simply wrong. Every real match set has them — the question is how many.

คู่ที่จับผิด · ของจริงมีเสมอ อยู่ที่ว่ามากแค่ไหน

One real matched pair · 66.3 is the number the matcher minimises

A · Feature Matching The obvious idea, and what it actually gives you
😬

"For each keypoint, take the closest descriptor" is exactly what this picture is — and only about 15% of those lines are right. A keypoint on a blank patch of cardboard has something nearest to it, and the matcher returns it with no hesitation. Nearest is not the same as correct.

1 / 59
A · Feature Matching Ask for a clear winner, not just a winner
keep if  d2nd​dbest​​<0.7

If the second-best candidate is nearly as close as the best, the descriptor is not distinctive here — it probably came from a repeated pattern, and picking either one is a coin flip. Throw it away.

💡

The test costs nothing: the matcher already found the two nearest candidates. The comparison, not the distance, is what carries the information.

1 / 59
A · Feature Matching Same pair, one line of filtering
✅

We threw away 88% of the matches and the picture got better. Of the 73 survivors, 71 turn out to be correct. Discarding data is not a loss when the data was noise.

A · Feature Matching Try it: move the threshold, watch the matches go

💡

These are the real matches from the previous slide's pair — green later confirmed by RANSAC, red rejected. The slider stops at 0.95, so only the 286 candidates that pass there are loaded; the other 318 of the 604 fail at every setting.

A · Feature Matching 🌍 Use case: matching, thirty times a second
1

Visual SLAM (Simultaneous Localisation and Mapping) — a robot works out both where it is and what the room looks like from matches between frames.

2

AR — a virtual object stays glued to a real table because the app re-matches features every frame.

⚡

At 30 frames per second SIFT is too slow, so phones use ORB with binary descriptors compared by Hamming distance — same idea, counting differing bits instead of measuring distance.

1 / 59
A · Feature Matching ↩ So how does the phone know?

It does not know

It proposes. Each keypoint's descriptor gets compared with every descriptor in the other photo, and the nearest one is a candidate.

Then it doubts

The ratio test drops every proposal that had a close runner-up — roughly nine out of ten of them.

And still doubts

Even the survivors are not all right. Sub-topic B is the machinery that copes with that — without ever identifying which ones are wrong.

🧠

This is the real lesson of computer vision as a discipline: you build reliable systems out of unreliable measurements, not by making the measurements perfect.

A · Feature Matching
💻 LAB — Match two real photos
①Fetch the classic OpenCV pair · ② detect and describe · ③ match, then filter
lab_a.pyColab · downloads two small images
import cv2, numpy as np
from urllib.request import urlretrieve
U = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/opencv/opencv/4.x/samples/data/"
for f in ("box.png", "box_in_scene.png"): urlretrieve(U+f, f)
a = cv2.imread("box.png", 0); b = cv2.imread("box_in_scene.png", 0)
sift = cv2.SIFT_create()
k1, d1 = sift.detectAndCompute(a, None)
k2, d2 = sift.detectAndCompute(b, None)
pairs = cv2.BFMatcher().knnMatch(d1, d2, k=2)      # best AND second best
good  = [m for m, n in pairs if m.distance < 0.7*n.distance]
print(len(k1), "keypoints", len(pairs), "candidates", len(good), "kept")
✅

Prints 604 keypoints · 604 candidates · 73 kept — draw them with cv2.drawMatches and you get the picture from two slides ago.

1 / 59
A · Feature Matching 🔍 Explore — what does the threshold actually cost?
explore_a.py
for r in [0.95, 0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.6, 0.5]:
    g = [m for m, n in pairs if m.distance < r*n.distance]
    src = np.float32([k1[m.queryIdx].pt for m in g]).reshape(-1,1,2)
    dst = np.float32([k2[m.trainIdx].pt for m in g]).reshape(-1,1,2)
    _, mask = cv2.findHomography(src, dst, cv2.RANSAC, 4.0)
    print(r, "kept", len(g), "correct", int(mask.sum()),
          "=", round(100*int(mask.sum())/len(g)), "%")
🔎

At 0.95 you keep 286 matches and only 31% are right; at 0.7 you keep 73 and 97% are right; at 0.5 you keep 43 and every one is right. Purity is bought with quantity — and since a homography needs only four correct pairs, buying purity is usually the right trade. Somewhere below that, though, you run out of matches entirely.

The right threshold depends on how much of the two images actually overlap — there is no universal 0.7.

B · RANSAC Key Terms — Robust Estimation

RANSAC

/ˈræn.sæk/ · RANdom SAmple Consensus

Guess a model from a tiny random sample, count who agrees, repeat, keep the most popular guess.

สุ่มตัวอย่างเล็ก ๆ มาสร้างโมเดล นับว่าใครเห็นด้วย ทำซ้ำ แล้วเก็บอันที่มีเสียงหนุนมากที่สุด

Inlier

/ˈɪn.laɪ.ər/

A data point that agrees with the model, within a chosen tolerance.

จุดที่เข้ากับโมเดลภายในระยะที่ยอมรับได้

Minimal sample

/ˈmɪn.ɪ.məl/

The fewest points that pin the model down: 2 for a line, 4 for a homography.

จำนวนจุดน้อยที่สุดที่กำหนดโมเดลได้ · เส้นตรง 2 · homography 4

Consensus

/kənˈsen.səs/

The set of inliers a candidate model attracts. The biggest consensus wins.

กลุ่มจุดที่เห็นด้วยกับโมเดลนั้น · กลุ่มใหญ่สุดชนะ

🔑

The trick behind the whole method: wrong points disagree with each other too. Outliers never accidentally line up into a large crowd, so the model with the biggest crowd is almost certainly built on the good data.

1 / 59
B · RANSAC Four steps, repeated until you get lucky
🎲

Same code, same 174 matches. What changes is the round it arrives on — and whether it arrives at all. That is what "until you get lucky" means: no step in the loop hunts for outliers, so slide 19 budgets rounds instead.

1 / 59
B · RANSAC Two rounds on the same eight points
1

A line needs two points, so the sample is two points, chosen at random.

2

Those two define one candidate line exactly — no fitting, no averaging.

3

Every other point is measured against it. Within the tolerance → inlier.

🏆

The unlucky round is not a problem — it simply loses the vote. Bad samples are self-eliminating, which is why the method needs no cleverness, only repetitions.

1 / 59
B · RANSAC How many repetitions is "enough"?
N=log(1−ws)log(1−p)​
Nhow many rounds — the formula's answer pconfidence you want — you choose (0.99) wthe good fraction, inliers ÷ total — measured, not set spoints per sample — the model fixes it (4 for H)
📌

It says: keep drawing until the chance of never once drawing a clean sample falls below 1%.

⚠️

The vertical axis is logarithmic, so that gentle-looking slope is an exponential cost: for a homography, every 20 points you lose off the inlier ratio multiplies the rounds by about 4, then 6, then 30. The three marked points are 71 rounds at 50%, 1,177 at 25% and 46,049 at 10% — the first two are nothing, the third is why the ratio test runs first.

1 / 59
B · RANSAC 🌍 RANSAC on the actual match set
A match is never plotted anywhere — the candidate H (a 3×3 map from photo 1 to photo 2 — sub-topic C unpacks it) turns it into one number: push (x,y) through H, then measure how far that prediction lands from the (x′,y′) the match claims. Those four numbers are all that enters — the 128-D descriptor found the match back in sub-topic A and is never looked at again.
(182,163) →H→ (192,253) = the match → 0.0 px · inlier(204,219) →H→ (198,286) ≠ (353,22) → 306 px · outlier
🎯

Half of these are wrong, and RANSAC sorted them knowing nothing about boxes or scenes: the green ones agree on one H, the red ones each propose something different and get outvoted. The same three lines of code do this for panoramas, AR tracking and medical scans.

1 / 59
B · RANSAC ↩ Fitting without knowing which points are bad

The answer to the opening question is almost anticlimactic: you never find the bad points. You find a model that does not need them.

Once you have the model, the outliers identify themselves.

How least squares gets its answer

One closed-form solve, no sampling and no repeats: the line that minimises ∑(yi​−(mxi​+c))2. The squaring is the whole story — a reading 3× further off pulls 12× harder, so the 8 blocked readings are 17% of the hook's data but 63% of the error being minimised.

RANSAC does not replace this solve — it postpones it. Steps ①–④ minimise nothing; a minimal sample leaves no error to minimise. The vote picks which points to trust, then this runs once on those — the hook's 0.81 is a least-squares fit, on 39 readings instead of 48.

🔁

Fit first, label second. Cleaning the data before you have a model is how people throw away the wrong things.

①Loosen the ratio test on purpose
②Fit with RANSAC

lab_b.pycontinues from lab_a.py
loose = [m for m, n in pairs if m.distance < 0.9*n.distance]   # leave junk in
src = np.float32([k1[m.queryIdx].pt for m in loose]).reshape(-1,1,2)
dst = np.float32([k2[m.trainIdx].pt for m in loose]).reshape(-1,1,2)
H, mask = cv2.findHomography(src, dst, cv2.RANSAC, 4.0)
print(len(loose), "matches in,", int(mask.sum()), "inliers out")
inl = [m for m, keep in zip(loose, mask.ravel()) if keep]
cv2.imwrite("inliers.png", cv2.drawMatches(a, k1, b, k2, inl, None))
✅

Prints 174 matches in, 86 inliers out. The mask is a column of 0/1 — one per match, in the order you passed them. It is the most useful thing the function returns and most people ignore it.

B · RANSAC 🔍 Explore — how forgiving should "agrees" be?

The last argument is the tolerance in pixels. Sweep it:

explore_b.py
for t in [1.0, 2.0, 4.0, 8.0, 20.0]:
    H, mask = cv2.findHomography(src, dst, cv2.RANSAC, t)
    print("tolerance", t, "px ->", int(mask.sum()), "inliers of", len(loose))
🔎

You get 78 · 86 · 86 · 87 · 91 inliers as the tolerance opens from 1 px to 20 px — it barely moves. That flatness is the result worth reading: these matches are either clearly right or clearly wrong, with almost nothing sitting in the grey zone between, so the exact tolerance hardly matters. When the count does climb steeply with tolerance, be suspicious — you are buying inliers by lowering the bar. A few pixels is the honest default either way.

C · Transforms & Homography Key Terms — Transforms

Affine

/ˈæf.aɪn/

Translation, rotation, scale and shear combined. Parallel lines stay parallel.

การแปลงที่รวมเลื่อน หมุน ย่อขยาย เฉือน — เส้นขนานยังขนานอยู่

Projective / Homography

/ˌprəˈdʒek.tɪv/ · /həˈmɒɡ.rə.fi/

The full perspective transform between two views of a flat surface. Parallel lines may converge.

การแปลงมุมมองเต็มรูประหว่างสองภาพของระนาบเดียวกัน — เส้นขนานบรรจบกันได้

Homogeneous coordinates

/ˌhɒm.əˈdʒiː.ni.əs/

Writing a point as (x,y,1) so that perspective becomes an ordinary matrix multiply.

เขียนจุดเป็น (x, y, 1) เพื่อให้เพอร์สเปกทีฟกลายเป็นการคูณเมทริกซ์ธรรมดา

Degrees of freedom (DOF)

/ˌdiː.oʊˈef/

How many independent numbers a transform has. More freedom = more shapes it can express, and more data needed to fix it.

จำนวนตัวเลขอิสระของการแปลง · อิสระมาก = ยืดหยุ่นมาก แต่ต้องใช้ข้อมูลมากขึ้น

🔑

The question is not "what is the formula" but "which one do I need, and what does it cost in matched points?"

C · Transforms & Homography A ladder of transforms — each rung adds freedom

Translation · 2

tx​ px across, ty​ px down

​100​010​tx​ty​1​​

bottom row locked

Rigid · 3

+ rotation; sizes unchanged

​cosθsinθ0​−sinθcosθ0​tx​ty​1​​

6 cells, but θ is one number → 3

Affine · 6

+ scale and shear

​ad0​be0​cf1​​

top two rows all yours

Projective · 8

+ perspective

​adg​beh​cf1​​

the bottom row opens up

⚖️

Climbing the ladder is not free, and it costs twice. More freedom fits more situations — and fits your noise more eagerly. It also costs RANSAC rounds: at 50% inliers a line takes 16, a homography 71. Use the lowest rung that can describe what actually happened between the two photos.

1 / 59
C · Transforms & Homography One glance tells affine from projective
📏

Parallel lines stay parallel → affine. A square never becomes a trapezoid, because its 3×3 bottom row is locked to [001] — the stretch is the same everywhere in the image.

🛤️

Parallel lines converge → projective. Rails meeting at the horizon. Its bottom row is [gh1] with g and h free, so the stretch changes across the image — that is the whole difference.

1 / 59
C · Transforms & Homography Applying one: multiply, then divide
​x′y′w′​​=H​xy1​​
H=​0.440−0.001−0.000256​−0.1610.407−0.000338​118.83161.001​​

the real H for the pair on slide 20 · orange = the bottom row's g and h

One real point, all the way through

① put a 1 on the end  →  [182, 163, 1]
② multiply by H  →  [172.7, 227.1, 0.898]
③ divide by w′  →  (192.2, 252.9)

Where does 0.898 come from? The bottom row you met last slide: w′=gx+hy+1. Here that is −0.0466−0.0551+1=0.898. The bottom row is the thing that computes w′ — that is its whole job.

Why affine feels simpler

Its bottom row is [001], so w′=1 everywhere and step ③ does nothing. That is the only reason nobody writes it down for affine.

w′ is not a constant

Across this one image it runs 1.000 at the top-left corner to 0.842 at the bottom-right. That drift is the perspective — far things shrink because they are divided by more.

❌

The most common bug in this pipeline: skipping ③. Read off [172.7, 227.1] and you get (173,227) instead of (192,253) — 32 px wrong, and the picture just comes out stretched.

1 / 59
C · Transforms & Homography How many matched points does each one need?
🧮

The rule behind the whole column: one matched pair gives you two equations — one for x′ and one for y′ — so ⌈DOF/2⌉ pairs give you at least as many equations as unknowns. The ceiling is doing work on one row: rigid has 3 unknowns but 2 pairs give 4 equations — one spare, because you cannot sample half a pair. The other three rows come out exact, which is why cv2.findHomography refuses to run on fewer than four points.

1 / 59
C · Transforms & Homography 🌍 Use case: putting the object back where it belongs
🎯

Nothing was detected here — the outline is four corners multiplied by a matrix. A rectangle came out as a tilted quadrilateral because the box is seen at an angle, which is precisely what a projective transform expresses. This one figure is what "object localisation by geometry" means, and it is the same operation behind AR overlays, product inspection and augmented posters.

1 / 59
C · Transforms & Homography ↩ So what does the scanner app need?
Whichprojective — the page edges converge
DOF8
Pairs⌈8 / 2⌉ = 4
∴ four corners is exactly enough

And that is why every scanner app asks you to drag four handles — not three, not five. The interface is the mathematics.

C · Transforms & Homography
💻 LAB — Write your own scanner app in six lines
①Name four corners
②Say where they should go
③Warp
lab_c.pyColab · no downloads needed
tilted = cv2.imread("tilted.png")          # or any photo of a page
src = np.float32([[70,20], [550,66], [516,436], [22,384])  # its 4 corners
W, Hh = 420, 340
dst = np.float32([[0,0], [W,0], [W,Hh], [0,Hh]])       # where they belong
M = cv2.getPerspectiveTransform(src, dst)          # 4 pairs -> one H
flat = cv2.warpPerspective(tilted, M, (W, Hh))
print(np.round(M, 4))     # bottom row prints [0. 0.0001 1.] — tiny, but not zero
✅

The page comes out rectangular and readable. Look at the printed bottom row — [0. 0.0001 1.]. Those digits look like rounding noise and they are not: that row is the perspective, and it is what makes w′ vary across the image. Set it to [001] by hand, warp again, and watch the correction fail.

1 / 59
C · Transforms & Homography 🔍 Explore — give it three points instead of four

The same corners, solved as an affine transform (3 pairs) and as a projective one (4 pairs):

explore_c.py
A = cv2.getAffineTransform(src[:3], dst[:3])     # 6 DOF, 3 pairs
P = cv2.getPerspectiveTransform(src, dst)          # 8 DOF, 4 pairs
aff  = cv2.warpAffine(tilted, A, (W, Hh))
proj = cv2.warpPerspective(tilted, P, (W, Hh))
# check where the FOURTH corner ends up under each transform
p = np.array([src[3][0], src[3][1], 1.0])
print("affine  ->", (A @ p).round(1))
q = P @ p
print("project ->", (q[:2]/q[2]).round(1), " (w =", round(q[2],3), ")")
🔎

The projective solution lands the fourth corner exactly on (0, 340) where it was asked to go; the affine one misses, because with 6 degrees of freedom it had already spent all of them on the first three pairs and has nothing left to satisfy the fourth. Three pairs cannot pin down eight numbers — the shortfall is not a bug in the code, it is arithmetic. Note the printed w′ too: it is not 1.

D · Stitching a Panorama Key Terms — Stitching

Warp

/wɔːrp/

Redrawing an image through a transform so it sits in the other image's frame.

วาดภาพใหม่ผ่านการแปลง เพื่อให้ไปอยู่ในกรอบพิกัดของอีกภาพ

Canvas

/ˈkæn.vəs/

The output image, made big enough to hold both photos after warping.

ผืนผ้าใบผลลัพธ์ — ต้องใหญ่พอรับทั้งสองภาพหลัง warp

Overlap

/ˌoʊ.vərˈlæp/

The region both photos cover. Matching needs it; blending happens inside it.

บริเวณที่สองภาพซ้อนกัน — ต้องมีถึงจะจับคู่ได้ และเป็นที่ที่ทำ blending

Blending (feathering)

/ˈfeð.ər.ɪŋ/

Fading from one image to the other across the overlap so the join stops being visible.

D · Stitching a Panorama Five steps, and you have met four of them
🧩

Worth pausing on: this session is one pipeline told backwards. We learned matching because stitching needs it, RANSAC because matching is unreliable, and homography because RANSAC needs a model to fit. Now they run forwards.

D · Stitching a Panorama Three sub-topics, one function call
the heart of the pipeline
H, mask = cv2.findHomography(pts1, pts2, cv2.RANSAC, 4.0)

pts1, pts2

the matches that survived the ratio test — sub-topic A

cv2.RANSAC

sample 4, fit, count, repeat — sub-topic B

4.0

the tolerance in pixels — how far off a point may land and still count as agreeing (slide 23)

H

a 3×3 projective matrix, 8 free numbers — sub-topic C

mask

which matches agreed — your quality report

📌

Why 4 points and not 3 or 10? Because a homography has 8 degrees of freedom and each pair gives 2 equations. The number in RANSAC's sampling loop comes straight from the previous sub-topic — these are not two separate facts to memorise. Two different fours live on this line: the 4 points per sample is fixed by the model and is not yours to choose; the 4.0 is pixels of tolerance and is.

D · Stitching a Panorama Geometry is not enough — the join still shows
📐

Warping aligns the geometry. After it, the same brick is at the same pixel in both images.

🎨

Blending hides the photography. The two shots had different exposure, so a hard paste leaves a visible step even when the alignment is perfect.

1 / 59
D · Stitching a Panorama 🌍 The two situations where this is allowed
⚠️

That third case is called parallax (pronounced "PA-ra-lax" /ˈpær.ə.læks/), and no single matrix can undo it — a near object and a far object need different transforms. This is why phone panoramas ask you to pivot on the spot, and why professional aerial mapping uses full 3D reconstruction instead of one homography.

1 / 59
D · Stitching a Panorama ↩ So why did the leaves tear?

90% of the matches agreed with the homography, which is why every number in the report looked healthy. They agreed because the bar is 4 px — and even the leaves only miss by about one.

But the plants sit much closer to the camera, so between the two viewpoints they slid further than the board did. One matrix cannot move two depths by different amounts.

🚨

The trap worth remembering: a high inlier ratio told us nothing here — a ratio cannot see an error smaller than its own tolerance. The layers are ~1 px apart, the bar is 4 px, so every layer passes and the count looks healthy while the picture tears.

D · Stitching a Panorama
💻 LAB — Stitch two photos end to end
①Match + RANSAC (you already have this)
②Warp onto a wide canvas
③Paste and look at the seam
lab_d.pytwo overlapping photos: yours, or the aloe pair
# H maps points of img2 into img1's frame (from findHomography)
h1, w1 = img1.shape[:2]; h2, w2 = img2.shape[:2]
canvas = cv2.warpPerspective(img2, H, (w1 + w2, max(h1, h2)))
canvas[:h1, :w1] = img1                       # hard paste, seam and all
xs = np.where(canvas.any(axis=(0, 2)))[0]      # trim the empty right side
cv2.imwrite("pano.png", canvas[:, xs.min():xs.max()+1])
✅

You get one wide image. Two things to notice before moving on: the canvas had to be made bigger than either input, and the line where the two meet is visible — the geometry is right and the photograph still looks wrong. That is what step ⑤ is for.

D · Stitching a Panorama 🔍 Explore — measure the tear instead of squinting at it

Do not trust the inlier count. Ask each match how far off it landed:

explore_d.py
proj = cv2.perspectiveTransform(src, H)             # where H says they go
err  = np.linalg.norm(proj - dst, axis=2).ravel()  # where they really are
print("median", round(np.median(err), 1),
      "| 90th pct", round(np.percentile(err, 90), 1),
      "| worst", round(err.max()))
# run this on a flat scene (a wall) and on a deep one (the aloe pair)
🔎

On the aloe pair: median 0.7 px, 90th percentile 4 px, worst 382 px. A flat scene gives a worst case of a few pixels, not hundreds. The gap between the median and the maximum is the parallax, and it is invisible in the inlier count — which is exactly why this three-line check belongs in your project.

Expected: the pivot pair stitches cleanly. The sideways pair aligns the far background and tears the near object, while the inlier ratio stays high in both cases. The number that warns you is the worst-case reprojection error, not the count. Report both in your project — and if you ever need the second case to work properly, you have left homography behind and entered 3D reconstruction.

Where you can use this 🌍 Lining up two views — at three different scales

Every one of these is the same pipeline: match, reject, transform, warp.

🗺️

Maps

The problem: millions of separate photos have to become one seamless surface.

What you learned: Street View and satellite mosaics are homographies, stitched at industrial scale with the same four-point rule.

street imagery · satellite mosaics · historical map overlays

🕶️

Augmented reality

The problem: a virtual object must stay glued to a real surface while the camera moves.

What you learned: match against the surface, estimate the transform, redraw — thirty times a second, with RANSAC absorbing the bad frames.

phone AR · virtual try-on · sports broadcast overlays

🛩️

Surveying & drones

The problem: hundreds of overlapping aerial photos have to become one measurable model.

What you learned: matching and RANSAC are the front half of photogrammetry — and because terrain has depth, this is exactly where a single homography must give way to 3D.

crop surveys · construction progress · disaster mapping

Where you can use this 🌍 And three where nothing is being stitched at all

📄 Documents

Every scanner app is four corners and one homography. The hard part is not the maths — it is finding the corners automatically, which is the edge detection from Session 4.

🏥 Medicine

Image registration: line up a scan taken today with one taken six months ago so a doctor is comparing the same tissue and not the same pixel. Alignment first, comparison second.

🔍 Inspection

To ask "does this part match the reference?" you must first put them in the same frame. Most defect-detection systems spend more code on aligning than on detecting.

🔁

Notice what all six domains have in common — the alignment is never the goal. It is the step that has to happen before the real question (what changed? what is defective? where am I?) can even be asked.

Where you can use this 🌍 Turning this into your own project
a good topic = two or more photos of the same thing + a reason they have to be lined up

"Stitch a panorama of the campus — and find where it breaks"

Shoot the same spot pivoting and then walking · report the error triple for both.

"De-skew and read a stack of receipts"

Corners → homography → OCR · measure how much rectification improves the text.

"Align two photos of the same plant, a week apart"

Register, subtract, and show what actually grew rather than what moved.

📥

What to show in the report: the inlier count and ratio, the reprojection error triple, the warped result — and one case where it failed, with your explanation of which assumption broke.

⚠️

Sanity-check before you commit: do your two photos actually overlap, and is the thing you care about flat? If not, you have a 3D project, which is a different and much larger one.

Summary Session Summary
Matching
nearest descriptor is only a proposal — the ratio test throws out the ambiguous ones, and on a hard pair that is 88% of them
RANSAC
sample the minimum, fit, count who agrees, repeat · it never identifies the outliers, it just finds a model that does not need them · N=log(1−p)/log(1−ws) rounds, cheap until the inlier ratio gets low
Transforms
translation 2 · rigid 3 · affine 6 · projective 8 DOF · parallels stay parallel below projective
Point pairs
⌈DOF/2⌉ — each match gives two equations, so a homography needs 4 · multiply, then divide by w′
Stitching
detect → match → RANSAC homography → warp → blend · valid for a flat scene or a camera that only turns
Judging it
inlier count, inlier ratio, and the reprojection error triple — a high ratio can still hide a torn picture

🧮Worked Example — Is This Result Good Enough?

The report

  • 1200 candidate matches
  • the ratio test keeps 180
  • RANSAC returns 45 inliers

The question

  • do we trust this homography?
Ignorethe 1200 — it counts keypoints, not agreement
Ratio45 / 180 = 25% inliers
Count45 ≫ 4, the minimum a homography needs
Roundsat w = 0.25, s = 4 → RANSAC needs ~1100 tries
∴ usable — but check the reprojection error too
❌

Reporting "1200 matches!" in a project write-up. The only two numbers that mean anything are the inlier count and the inlier ratio — and below roughly 10% the result is usually rubbish.

1 / 59
✎Quick Check — How Many Rounds?⏱ 3 min

Half of your matches are outliers and you are fitting a homography. Roughly how many RANSAC rounds do you need for a 99% chance of drawing one clean sample — and what happens to that number if you fit an affine transform instead?

✅

About 72 rounds — 0.5⁴ = 1/16, so a clean sample turns up roughly once every 16 tries and 72 makes missing it unlikely. An affine transform needs only 3 points, so 0.5³ = 1/8 and about 35 rounds suffice. Fewer degrees of freedom means a smaller sample, which means far less luck required — one more reason not to climb the ladder without a reason.

1 / 59
🧮Worked Example — Which Transform, and How Many Points
Leftparallels preserved → affine, 6 DOF
⌈6 / 2⌉ = 3 point pairs
Rightparallels converge → projective, 8 DOF
⌈8 / 2⌉ = 4 point pairs
∴ look at the parallels, count the DOF, halve it
❌

Answering "8 points" for a homography. The 8 is degrees of freedom, not points — each pair supplies two equations, so four pairs cover it.

1 / 59
✎Quick Check — Poster on a Wall⏱ 3 min

You want to paste a rectangular poster into a photo of a wall that recedes into the distance, so it looks like it is really there. (a) Which transform, and how many point pairs? (b) The client now asks for the poster on a curved pillar instead. What changes?

✅

(a) Projective — a homography, 8 DOF, 4 point pairs. The wall is flat and the perspective makes its parallel edges converge, which is exactly what the extra two degrees of freedom over affine buy you.  (b) A homography no longer applies. A curved surface is not a plane, so no single 3×3 matrix can describe it — you would need to model the surface and warp along it. Recognising that a method does not apply is the more valuable half of knowing it.

🧮Worked Example — Pushing a Point Through H

Given

  • the point (2, 3) in image 1
  • H = [[1, 0, 4],
         [0, 1, 2],
         [0, 0.5, 1]]

Find

  • where it lands in image 2
Step 1write it as [2, 3, 1]
x'1(2) + 0(3) + 4(1) = 6
y'0(2) + 1(3) + 2(1) = 5
w'0(2) + 0.5(3) + 1(1) = 2.5
Divide(6 / 2.5, 5 / 2.5) = (2.4, 2)
∴ (2, 3) → (2.4, 2)
❌

Stopping at (6, 5). That bottom row [0, 0.5, 1] is what makes this projective rather than affine — skip the divide and you have silently used the wrong transform.

Topics pulled in: ratio test · inliers vs matches · DOF and point pairs · the planarity assumption

📋The Case — A Classroom Panorama That Came Out Wrong

What happened

  • A student swept a phone across the classroom from one spot and shot two photos.
  • The back wall lines up beautifully; the desk in the foreground appears twice.
  • Their log: 900 candidates → 30 kept → 24 inliers

Answer these

  • Q1 — which transform is right for two photos taken from one spot, and how many pairs does it need?
  • Q2 — the ratio test kept only 30 of 900. Is that alarming? What would you check?
  • Q3 — 24 inliers of 30 is 80%. Why did the desk still double?
  • Q4 — name one change to how the photos are taken that would fix it.
💭

Work in the order the pipeline runs — matches, then inliers, then the transform, then the assumption behind it.

✔Part A — Answers
Q1Projective — a homography, 8 DOF, 4 point pairs. Pivoting on one spot is
exactly the case a homography is valid for, whatever the depth of the scene.
Q230 of 900 is low but not fatal — 24 inliers is plenty for a 4-point model.
Check the overlap: too little shared view is the usual cause.
Q3Because they did not really pivot — they moved sideways as well. The 24
inliers all sit on the far wall and agree; the near desk needed a different
shift and got outvoted. 80% inliers, still a wrong picture.
Q4Rotate the phone about its own axis without stepping sideways — or stand
further back so nothing is close, and increase the overlap while you are at it.
🧠

Q3 is the one that matters. Every number in the log looked fine. The fault was not in the code or the thresholds — it was in an assumption the code cannot check for you.

💻Q5 — The Report Your Project Should Print
case.pyfill in the TODOs
def alignment_report(src, dst, H, mask):
    # TODO 1: inlier count and inlier ratio
    # TODO 2: reprojection error of the inliers — median, 90th pct, max
    # TODO 3: print one line: n / ratio / median / p90 / max
    # TODO 4: return a verdict string — "ok", "too few matches",
    #         or "depth varies — one H cannot cover it" when max is huge, median tiny
    ...
✅

Expected on the aloe pair: n=969 · ratio=0.90 · median=0.7 · p90=4.0 · max=382 → "depth varies — one H cannot cover it". Four numbers, one verdict, six lines of code. This is the difference between a project that shows a nice panorama and one that can say why the other panorama failed — and the second is what gets marked.
